about: Ext 2 (4U) revision questions transcribed from post-2019 NSW trial papers on thsconline (Ext 2 trials base 5348; Ext 1 trials base 5338 for t-formulae, product-to-sum, inverse trig and vectors, which Jamie's school counts as 4U). 'q' and 'sol' are HTML with KaTeX $...$; 'sol' is Claude's worked solution. qpage = question page, spage = first page of the official solutions section (null = unknown, use page 1). Topics: complex, t-formulae, product-to-sum, inverse trig, vectors, proof, integration, mechanics. Multiple-choice questions were rewritten as short answers.

items.q: Find $\dfrac{-3+i}{1-2i}$, showing all working out.
items.sol:
Multiply top and bottom by the conjugate $1+2i$:
$\dfrac{(-3+i)(1+2i)}{(1-2i)(1+2i)}=\dfrac{-3-6i+i+2i^2}{1+4}=\dfrac{-5-5i}{5}=-1-i$.

items.q: Given that $w=2-i\left(2\sqrt3\right)$ and $\operatorname{Arg}(zw)=\dfrac{\pi}{3}$, find the exact value of $\operatorname{Arg}(z)$.
items.sol:
$\operatorname{Arg}(w)=\tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac{-2\sqrt3}{2}\right)=-\frac{\pi}{3}$ (4th quadrant).
$\operatorname{Arg}(z)=\operatorname{Arg}(zw)-\operatorname{Arg}(w)=\frac{\pi}{3}+\frac{\pi}{3}=\frac{2\pi}{3}$, which is already in $(-\pi,\pi]$.

items.q: The complex numbers $z_1=2-3i$, $z_2$ and $z_3$ are roots of $p(z)=z^3-8z^2+29z-52$. Find $z_2$ and $z_3$.
items.sol:
Real coefficients, so the conjugate is also a root: $z_2=2+3i$.
Sum of roots $=8$: $z_3=8-(2-3i)-(2+3i)=4$.
Check with the product: $(2-3i)(2+3i)\cdot4=13\cdot4=52$ ✓.

items.q: Find the square roots of $21-20i$.

Points $A(z_1)$ and $B(z_2)$ on an Argand diagram satisfy $OA=2\,OB$ and $\angle AOB=\frac{\pi}{6}$, with $B$ anticlockwise from $A$. Also $z_1=r(\cos\theta+i\sin\theta)$, $0<\theta<\frac{\pi}{2}$.
(i) Express $z_2$ in exponential form in terms of $r$ and $\theta$. [2]
(ii) $C$ is the point such that $ABOC$ is a parallelogram and $\angle AOC=\phi$, $0<\phi<\frac{\pi}{2}$. $C$ is represented by $z_1w$. By finding $w$, calculate $\phi$ to two decimal places. [3] (The original has a diagram; open the paper to see it.)
items.sol:
(i) $|z_2|=\frac r2$ and $\arg z_2=\theta+\frac\pi6$, so $z_2=\frac r2 e^{i(\theta+\pi/6)}$.
(ii) Opposite sides are equal and parallel: $\overrightarrow{OC}=\overrightarrow{BA}$, so $z_1w=z_1-z_2=re^{i\theta}\left(1-\tfrac12e^{i\pi/6}\right)$.
So $w=1-\tfrac12e^{i\pi/6}=\left(1-\tfrac{\sqrt3}{4}\right)-\tfrac14 i$, and $\arg w=-\tan^{-1}\frac{1/4}{1-\sqrt3/4}\approx-0.42$.
$C$ is clockwise from $A$ by $|\arg w|$, so $\phi\approx0.42$ radians.

items.q:
Consider the region defined by $|z-2+2i|\le4$ and $-\frac{\pi}{3}\le\operatorname{Arg}(z-1+3i)\le\frac{\pi}{4}$.
(i) Sketch the region. [3]
(ii) Let $w$ be any complex number in the region. Find the possible range of $\operatorname{Arg}(w)$, to two decimal places. [3]
items.sol:
(i) A disc with centre $2-2i$ and radius 4, cut by two rays from the excluded point $1-3i$ at angles $\frac\pi4$ and $-\frac\pi3$. The region is the slice of the disc between the rays.
(ii) The minimum is approached at the vertex $1-3i$ itself. That point is excluded, so the minimum is never reached: $\operatorname{Arg}(1-3i)\approx-1.25$.
The maximum is where the $\frac\pi4$ ray ($y=x-4$) meets the circle: $(x-2)^2+(x-2)^2=16\Rightarrow x=2+2\sqrt2$, $y=-2+2\sqrt2$, with $\operatorname{Arg}\approx0.17$.
So $-1.25<\operatorname{Arg}(w)\le0.17$.

items.q:
Let $C=1+\cos\theta+\cos2\theta+\dots+\cos(n-1)\theta$ and $S=\sin\theta+\sin2\theta+\dots+\sin(n-1)\theta$, with $z=\cos\theta+i\sin\theta$.
(i) Show that $C+iS=\dfrac{1-z^n}{1-z}$, $z\ne1$. [2]
(ii) Hence show that $\sin\theta+\sin2\theta+\dots+\sin(n-1)\theta=\dfrac{(\sin\theta-\sin n\theta)+\sin[(n-1)\theta]}{2(1-\cos\theta)}$. [2]
items.sol:
(i) By De Moivre, $C+iS=1+z+z^2+\dots+z^{n-1}$, a geometric series with ratio $z\ne1$, so it equals $\frac{1-z^n}{1-z}$.
(ii) Multiply top and bottom by $1-\bar z$. The denominator is $|1-z|^2=(1-\cos\theta)^2+\sin^2\theta=2(1-\cos\theta)$.
The numerator is $(1-z^n)(1-\bar z)=1-\bar z-z^n+z^{n-1}$, using $z\bar z=1$.
Its imaginary part is $\sin\theta-\sin n\theta+\sin(n-1)\theta$. Equate imaginary parts to get $S$.

items.q:
Let $\operatorname{Im}(z)\ne0$. Which is equivalent to $\dfrac{8\bar z z}{(\bar z-z)^2}$?
(A) $2+2\left(\frac{\operatorname{Re}z}{\operatorname{Im}z}\right)^2$   (B) $2+2\left(\frac{\operatorname{Im}z}{\operatorname{Re}z}\right)^2$   (C) $-2-2\left(\frac{\operatorname{Re}z}{\operatorname{Im}z}\right)^2$   (D) $-2-2\left(\frac{\operatorname{Im}z}{\operatorname{Re}z}\right)^2$
items.sol:
Let $z=x+iy$. Then $\bar zz=x^2+y^2$ and $(\bar z-z)^2=(-2iy)^2=-4y^2$.
So the expression is $\frac{8(x^2+y^2)}{-4y^2}=-2-2\left(\frac xy\right)^2$. (C)

items.q:
Let $z=5-12i$ and $w=3+4i$. Find:
(i) $v$ such that $3\bar v=z-2\bar w$ [2]
(ii) $\dfrac2w+z$ [1]
(iii) $u$ such that $u$ is a square root of $zw$, in the form $a+ib$ with $a>0$. [3]
Find $k\in\mathbb R$ so that there are only two points of intersection between $\left|\operatorname{Arg}(z-k-i)-\frac{\pi}{6}\right|\ge\frac{\pi}{6}$ and $|z-2-2i|=1$.
items.sol:
The inequality means $\operatorname{Arg}(z-(k+i))\ge\frac\pi3$ or $\le0$. So the region is everything except the wedge $0<\operatorname{Arg}(z-(k+i))<\frac\pi3$ with vertex $A=k+i$.
The circle (centre $2+2i$, radius 1) touches $\operatorname{Im}z=1$ at $B=2+i$. For only two intersections, the circle must sit inside the wedge, tangent to both rays.
By symmetry the centre is on the bisector, so $\angle BAC=\frac\pi6$ and $AB=\frac{1}{\tan(\pi/6)}=\sqrt3$.
So $k=2-\sqrt3$.

items.q:
(i) Using De Moivre's theorem, prove that $\cos6\theta=32\cos^6\theta-48\cos^4\theta+18\cos^2\theta-1$. [3]
(ii) Hence, by substituting $x=A\cos\theta$ for suitable $A$, or otherwise, find all roots of $P(x)=x^6-6x^4+9x^2-2$. [3]
items.sol:
(i) Take the real part of $(c+is)^6$: $\cos6\theta=c^6-15c^4s^2+15c^2s^4-s^6$. Substitute $s^2=1-c^2$ and simplify to $32c^6-48c^4+18c^2-1$.
(ii) With $x=2\cos\theta$: $P=64c^6-96c^4+36c^2-2=2\cos6\theta$.
So $P=0\iff\cos6\theta=0\iff\theta=\frac{\pi}{12},\frac{\pi}{4},\frac{5\pi}{12},\frac{7\pi}{12},\frac{3\pi}{4},\frac{11\pi}{12}$.
Roots: $x=\pm2\cos\frac{\pi}{12},\ \pm\sqrt2,\ \pm2\cos\frac{5\pi}{12}$, i.e. $\pm\frac{\sqrt6+\sqrt2}{2},\pm\sqrt2,\pm\frac{\sqrt6-\sqrt2}{2}$.

items.q:
A complex number $z$ satisfies $z^5+i=0$, $z\ne-i$.
(i) Show $z^4-iz^3-z^2+iz+1=0$. [1]
(ii) Prove $(z+i)\left(z^2+2iz\sin\frac{\pi}{10}-1\right)\left(z^2-2iz\sin\frac{3\pi}{10}-1\right)=0$. [3]
(iii) Hence prove $\sin\frac{\pi}{10}-\sin\frac{3\pi}{10}=-\frac12$. [2]
(iv) Hence find the exact values of $\sin\frac{\pi}{10}$ and $\sin\frac{3\pi}{10}$. [3]
items.sol:
(i) $z^5+i=(z+i)(z^4-iz^3-z^2+iz+1)$, and $z\ne-i$.
(ii) The roots of $z^5=-i$ are $e^{i\alpha}$ with $\alpha=-\frac\pi2,-\frac\pi{10},\frac{3\pi}{10},\frac{7\pi}{10},-\frac{9\pi}{10}$.
Pair $-\frac\pi{10}$ with $-\frac{9\pi}{10}$: their sum is $-2i\sin\frac\pi{10}$ and product $e^{-i\pi}=-1$.
Pair $\frac{3\pi}{10}$ with $\frac{7\pi}{10}$: their sum is $2i\sin\frac{3\pi}{10}$ and product $-1$. This gives the two quadratics.
(iii) Let $a=\sin\frac\pi{10}$, $b=\sin\frac{3\pi}{10}$. Compare $z^3$ coefficients: $2i(a-b)=-i\Rightarrow a-b=-\frac12$.
(iv) Compare $z^2$ coefficients: $-2+4ab=-1\Rightarrow ab=\frac14$. Solving gives $a=\frac{\sqrt5-1}{4}$ and $b=\frac{\sqrt5+1}{4}$.

items.q: Use the substitution $t=\tan\frac{\theta}{2}$ to find $\displaystyle\int\operatorname{cosec}\theta\,d\theta$.
items.sol:
$\sin\theta=\frac{2t}{1+t^2}$ and $d\theta=\frac{2\,dt}{1+t^2}$.
So $\int\frac{1+t^2}{2t}\cdot\frac{2}{1+t^2}\,dt=\int\frac{dt}{t}=\ln|t|+C=\ln\left|\tan\frac\theta2\right|+C$.
(The official solutions in this paper are handwritten scans near the back.)

items.q: By using an appropriate $t$-formula substitution, solve $3\cos\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right)-\sin\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right)=-3$ for $0\le\theta\le2\pi$.
items.sol:
Let $t=\tan\frac{\theta}{4}$. Then $\cos\frac\theta2=\frac{1-t^2}{1+t^2}$ and $\sin\frac\theta2=\frac{2t}{1+t^2}$.
$3(1-t^2)-2t=-3(1+t^2)\Rightarrow-2t=-6\Rightarrow t=3$, so $\frac\theta4=\tan^{-1}3$ and $\theta\approx5.00$.
Test the excluded case: $t$ is undefined at $\frac\theta4=\frac\pi2$, i.e. $\theta=2\pi$. There, $3\cos\pi-\sin\pi=-3$ ✓.
So $\theta\approx5.00$ or $\theta=2\pi$.

items.q: Using the substitution $t=\tan\frac{x}{2}$, solve $2-3\sin x+2\cos x=0$ for $0\le x\le2\pi$. Round to two decimal places where necessary.
items.sol:
$2(1+t^2)-6t+2(1-t^2)=0\Rightarrow4-6t=0\Rightarrow t=\frac23$, so $x=2\tan^{-1}\frac23\approx1.18$.
Test $x=\pi$ (where $t$ is undefined): $2-0+2(-1)=0$ ✓.
So $x\approx1.18$ or $x=\pi\approx3.14$.

items.q: Use the substitution $t=\tan\frac{\theta}{2}$ to solve $2\sin\theta+\cos\theta=2$ for $0\le\theta\le2\pi$.
items.sol:
$4t+(1-t^2)=2(1+t^2)\Rightarrow3t^2-4t+1=0\Rightarrow t=1$ or $t=\frac13$.
So $\theta=\frac\pi2$ or $\theta=2\tan^{-1}\frac13\approx0.644$.
Check $\theta=\pi$: $0-1\ne2$, so it's not a solution.

items.q: By making the substitution $t=\tan\frac{\theta}{2}$, or otherwise, show that $\operatorname{cosec}\theta+\cot\theta=\cot\frac{\theta}{2}$.
items.sol: $\operatorname{cosec}\theta+\cot\theta=\frac{1+t^2}{2t}+\frac{1-t^2}{2t}=\frac{2}{2t}=\frac1t=\cot\frac\theta2$.

items.q: Solve $2\operatorname{cosec}\theta-4\cot\theta=3$ using the $t$-formula, for $0\le\theta\le2\pi$. Give answers to 3 significant figures.
items.sol:
$\frac{1+t^2}{t}-\frac{2(1-t^2)}{t}=3\Rightarrow3t^2-3t-1=0\Rightarrow t=\frac{3\pm\sqrt{21}}{6}$.
For $t\approx1.264$: $\theta\approx1.80$. For $t\approx-0.264$: $\frac\theta2$ is in the 2nd quadrant, so $\theta\approx5.77$.
$\theta=\pi$ is excluded because $\operatorname{cosec}\pi$ is undefined. Answers: $1.80,\ 5.77$.

items.source: North Sydney Boys 2025 Ext 1 Task, Q12(b)
items.q:
(i) Use $t$-formulae to show $\dfrac{1-\cos\theta}{\sin\theta}=\tan\dfrac{\theta}{2}$. [1]
(ii) Hence find the exact value of $\tan15^\circ$. [1]
items.sol:
(i) $\dfrac{1-\frac{1-t^2}{1+t^2}}{\frac{2t}{1+t^2}}=\dfrac{2t^2}{2t}=t=\tan\frac\theta2$.
(ii) With $\theta=30^\circ$: $\tan15^\circ=\dfrac{1-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}}{\frac12}=2-\sqrt3$.

items.q:
(i) Let $t=\tan\left(\frac x2\right)$. Prove that $\frac12\cot\left(\frac x2\right)-\cot x=\frac12\tan\left(\frac x2\right)$. [2]
(ii) Prove by induction for all $n\ge1$: $\frac12\tan\frac x2+\frac14\tan\frac x4+\dots+\frac1{2^n}\tan\frac x{2^n}=\frac1{2^n}\cot\frac x{2^n}-\cot x$. [3]
items.sol:
(i) $\frac1{2t}-\frac{1-t^2}{2t}=\frac{t^2}{2t}=\frac t2$.
(ii) $n=1$ is part (i). Assume the result for $n=k$ and add $\frac1{2^{k+1}}\tan\frac x{2^{k+1}}$.
Apply (i) with $x\to\frac x{2^k}$ and multiply by $\frac1{2^k}$: $\frac1{2^{k+1}}\tan\frac x{2^{k+1}}=\frac1{2^{k+1}}\cot\frac x{2^{k+1}}-\frac1{2^k}\cot\frac x{2^k}$.
The $\frac1{2^k}\cot\frac x{2^k}$ terms cancel, leaving $\frac1{2^{k+1}}\cot\frac x{2^{k+1}}-\cot x$ ✓.

items.q: By use of a product-to-sum identity, find $\displaystyle\int\cos2x\sin3x\,dx$.
items.sol:
$\sin A\cos B=\frac12[\sin(A+B)+\sin(A-B)]$ with $A=3x$, $B=2x$: $\cos2x\sin3x=\frac12(\sin5x+\sin x)$.
So the integral is $-\frac1{10}\cos5x-\frac12\cos x+C$.

items.q: Find $\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/2}\sin5x\cos3x\,dx$.
items.sol:
$\sin5x\cos3x=\frac12(\sin8x+\sin2x)$.
$\frac12\left[-\frac{\cos8x}{8}-\frac{\cos2x}{2}\right]_0^{\pi/2}=\frac12\left[\left(-\frac18+\frac12\right)-\left(-\frac18-\frac12\right)\right]=\frac12$.

items.q: Find $\displaystyle\int3\cos(2x)\cos\left(5x-\frac{\pi}{3}\right)dx$.
items.sol:
$\cos A\cos B=\frac12[\cos(A+B)+\cos(A-B)]$: the integrand is $\frac32\left[\cos\left(7x-\frac\pi3\right)+\cos\left(3x-\frac\pi3\right)\right]$.
So the integral is $\frac3{14}\sin\left(7x-\frac\pi3\right)+\frac12\sin\left(3x-\frac\pi3\right)+C$.

items.q: Use the product to sum identity to write $\cos\theta\sin(2\theta)$ as a sum in simplest form.
items.sol: $\sin2\theta\cos\theta=\frac12[\sin3\theta+\sin\theta]$.

items.source: North Sydney Girls 2026 Ext 1 Trial, MC Q7
items.q: How many distinct solutions does $\sin x+\sin3x=\sin2x$ have for $0\le x\le2\pi$? (A) 5 (B) 6 (C) 7 (D) 8
items.sol:
Sum-to-product: $\sin3x+\sin x=2\sin2x\cos x$, so $\sin2x(2\cos x-1)=0$.
$\sin2x=0$ gives $x=0,\frac\pi2,\pi,\frac{3\pi}2,2\pi$ (5 solutions). $\cos x=\frac12$ gives $\frac\pi3,\frac{5\pi}3$ (2 solutions). They're all distinct, so 7. (C)

items.q:
(i) Prove that $\cos5x-\cos x=-2\sin2x\sin3x$. [2]
(ii) Hence solve $\cos5x-\cos x=\sin3x$ for $0\le x\le\pi$, giving exact answers. [3]
items.sol:
(i) $\cos(A+B)-\cos(A-B)=-2\sin A\sin B$. With $A=3x$, $B=2x$ this gives the result.
(ii) $-2\sin2x\sin3x=\sin3x\Rightarrow\sin3x(1+2\sin2x)=0$.
$\sin3x=0$: $x=0,\frac\pi3,\frac{2\pi}3,\pi$. $\sin2x=-\frac12$: $2x=\frac{7\pi}6,\frac{11\pi}6$, so $x=\frac{7\pi}{12},\frac{11\pi}{12}$.

items.q:
Let $\underset{\sim}{u}=2\underset{\sim}{i}+5\underset{\sim}{j}$ and $\underset{\sim}{v}=-3\underset{\sim}{i}+\lambda^2\underset{\sim}{j}$, $\lambda\in\mathbb R$.
(i) Find $\lambda$ such that $u$ and $v$ are perpendicular. [2]
(ii) Explain why $u$ cannot be parallel to $v$. [2]
(iii) If $\lambda=1$, find $q$ such that $u=\operatorname{proj}_v(u)+q$. [3]
items.sol:
(i) $u\cdot v=-6+5\lambda^2=0\Rightarrow\lambda=\pm\sqrt{6/5}$.
(ii) Parallel would need $\frac{-3}{2}=\frac{\lambda^2}{5}$, i.e. $\lambda^2=-\frac{15}2<0$. That's impossible for real $\lambda$.
(iii) $v=-3i+j$ and $u\cdot v=-1$, $|v|^2=10$, so $\operatorname{proj}_v u=-\frac1{10}v=0.3i-0.1j$.
So $q=u-\operatorname{proj}_vu=1.7i+5.1j$ (check: $q\cdot v=-5.1+5.1=0$ ✓).

items.q:
$P,Q$ have position vectors $\underset{\sim}{p},\underset{\sim}{q}$; $\overrightarrow{QR}=\frac32\overrightarrow{OP}$; $M$ is the intersection of $PQ$ and $OR$ with $PM:MQ=\lambda:1$ and $OM:MR=\mu:1$.
(i) Show $\overrightarrow{OM}=\frac{\mu}{\mu+1}\left(\frac32p+q\right)$. [1]
(ii) Show $\overrightarrow{OM}=p+\frac{\lambda}{\lambda+1}(q-p)$. [1]
(iii) Prove $\lambda=\frac23$ and hence $\overrightarrow{OM}=\frac35p+\frac25q$. [3] (The original has a diagram.)
items.sol:
(i) $\overrightarrow{OR}=q+\frac32p$, and $M$ divides $OR$ in the ratio $\mu:1$.
(ii) $M$ divides $PQ$ in the ratio $\lambda:1$.
(iii) $p,q$ are non-parallel, so equate coefficients. For $q$: $\frac{\mu}{\mu+1}=\frac{\lambda}{\lambda+1}$. For $p$: $\frac32\cdot\frac{\mu}{\mu+1}=1-\frac{\lambda}{\lambda+1}=\frac1{\lambda+1}$.
So $\frac32\lambda=1$, giving $\lambda=\frac23$, and $\overrightarrow{OM}=p+\frac25(q-p)=\frac35p+\frac25q$.

items.source: North Sydney Boys 2025 Ext 1 Task, Q12(d)
items.q: Solve $5\cos\left(x+\tan^{-1}\frac43\right)=0.5$ for $0\le x\le2\pi$, correct to 2 decimal places.
items.sol:
$\cos(x+\alpha)=0.1$ with $\alpha=\tan^{-1}\frac43\approx0.9273$, and $x+\alpha\in[\alpha,2\pi+\alpha]$.
$x+\alpha=\cos^{-1}0.1\approx1.4706$ or $2\pi-1.4706\approx4.8126$.
So $x\approx0.54$ or $x\approx3.89$.

items.q:
It is known that $5+6i$ is a zero of $P(z)=2z^3-19z^2+112z+k$, where $k$ is real.
(i) Find the other two zeroes of $P(z)$. [2]
(ii) Find the value of $k$. [1]
items.sol:
(i) Real coefficients, so $5-6i$ is also a zero. Sum of zeroes $=\frac{19}{2}$, so the third is $\frac{19}{2}-10=-\frac12$.
(ii) Product of zeroes $=-\frac k2$: $(5+6i)(5-6i)(-\tfrac12)=61\cdot(-\tfrac12)$, so $k=61$.
Check: sum of pairs $=61+(-\tfrac12)(10)=56=\frac{112}{2}$ ✓

items.q:
Let $z=1+i\sqrt3$.
(i) Express $z$ in modulus-argument form. [2]
(ii) Hence, simplify $z^{10}+512z$. [2]
items.sol:
(i) $|z|=2$, $\arg z=\frac\pi3$, so $z=2\operatorname{cis}\frac\pi3$.
(ii) $z^{10}=1024\operatorname{cis}\frac{10\pi}3=1024\operatorname{cis}\left(-\frac{2\pi}3\right)=-512-512\sqrt3\,i$, and $512z=512+512\sqrt3\,i$. So $z^{10}+512z=0$.

items.q:
Let $z=1+ai$ and $w=a+i$, where $a\in\mathbb R$. Find:
(i) $z+\overline w$. [1]
(ii) $\operatorname{Arg}(zw)$. [2]
(iii) the value(s) of $a$ for which $\dfrac zw$ is purely real. [2]
items.sol:
(i) $z+\overline w=(1+ai)+(a-i)=(1+a)+(a-1)i$.
(ii) $zw=(1+ai)(a+i)=a+i+a^2i-a=(1+a^2)i$, which lies on the positive imaginary axis, so $\operatorname{Arg}(zw)=\frac\pi2$.
(iii) $\dfrac zw=\dfrac{(1+ai)(a-i)}{a^2+1}=\dfrac{2a+(a^2-1)i}{a^2+1}$. Purely real when $a^2=1$, i.e. $a=\pm1$.

items.source: Abbotsleigh 2025 Trial, MC Q2 (as short answer)
items.q: A monic cubic $P(z)$ has real coefficients. $z=3$ and $z=2+i$ are roots of $P(z)=0$. Find $P(z)$ in expanded form.

The complex numbers $w$ and $z$ are given by $w=2e^{\frac{i\pi}{6}}$ and $z=10e^{\frac{i\pi}{3}}$.
(i) Find the modulus and argument of $wz$. [2]
(ii) Find, in Cartesian form, $\dfrac{z}{w^5}$. [2]
items.sol:
(i) $wz=20e^{i(\frac\pi6+\frac\pi3)}=20e^{\frac{i\pi}2}$: modulus $20$, argument $\frac\pi2$.
(ii) $w^5=32e^{\frac{5i\pi}6}$, so $\dfrac z{w^5}=\dfrac{10}{32}e^{i(\frac\pi3-\frac{5\pi}6)}=\dfrac5{16}e^{-\frac{i\pi}2}=-\dfrac5{16}i$.

items.q: The complex numbers $z$ and $w$ are given by $z=2\operatorname{cis}\frac\pi6$ and $w=3\operatorname{cis}\frac{2\pi}3$. Find the modulus and argument of $\dfrac zw$.
items.sol: $\left|\dfrac zw\right|=\dfrac23$ and $\arg\dfrac zw=\dfrac\pi6-\dfrac{2\pi}3=-\dfrac\pi2$.

items.source: Caringbah 2025 Trial, MC Q2 (as short answer)
items.q: If $z=\dfrac{3+4i}{1+2i}$, find the imaginary part of $z$.
items.sol: $z=\dfrac{(3+4i)(1-2i)}{5}=\dfrac{11-2i}5$, so $\operatorname{Im}(z)=-\dfrac25$.

items.q: Given $i(\omega+2)=z$ and $\omega z=-4i$, where $\operatorname{Im}(\omega)<0$, find the exact values of $\omega$ and $z$ in the form $a+ib$, where $a$ and $b$ are real.
items.sol:
Substitute: $\omega\cdot i(\omega+2)=-4i\Rightarrow\omega^2+2\omega+4=0\Rightarrow\omega=-1\pm i\sqrt3$. Since $\operatorname{Im}\omega<0$, $\omega=-1-i\sqrt3$.
Then $z=i(1-i\sqrt3)=\sqrt3+i$.
Check: $(-1-i\sqrt3)(\sqrt3+i)=-\sqrt3-i-3i+\sqrt3=-4i$ ✓

items.q:
(i) Show that $z^5-1=(z-1)(z^4+z^3+z^2+z+1)$. [1]
(ii) If $\omega$ is a complex root of $z^5-1=0$, show that $1+\omega^2+\omega^3=-(\omega+\omega^4)$. [1]
(iii) Hence show that $\cos\dfrac{2\pi}5+\dfrac12=\cos\dfrac\pi5$. [2]
items.sol:
(i) Expand: $(z-1)(z^4+z^3+z^2+z+1)=z^5-1$ (the middle terms telescope).
(ii) $\omega\ne1$ and $\omega^5=1$, so $\omega^4+\omega^3+\omega^2+\omega+1=0$; rearrange.
(iii) Take $\omega=\operatorname{cis}\frac{2\pi}5$. Then $\omega^4=\overline\omega$, so $\omega+\omega^4=2\cos\frac{2\pi}5$, and $\omega^3=\overline{\omega^2}$, so $\omega^2+\omega^3=2\cos\frac{4\pi}5=-2\cos\frac\pi5$.
So $1-2\cos\frac\pi5=-2\cos\frac{2\pi}5$, i.e. $\cos\frac{2\pi}5+\frac12=\cos\frac\pi5$.

items.q:
$P(z)=z^4-10z^3+117z^2-412z+1460$ has zeroes $2a+bi$ and $3a+2bi$, where $a$ and $b$ are integers.
(i) Find the values of $a$ and $b$, and hence find all the zeroes of $P(z)$. [3]
(ii) Factorise $P(z)$ into quadratic factors with real coefficients. [1]
items.sol:
(i) Real coefficients, so the conjugates are also zeroes. Sum of zeroes: $2(2a)+2(3a)=10a=10$, so $a=1$.
The quadratic factors are $z^2-4z+(4+b^2)$ and $z^2-6z+(9+4b^2)$. Matching the $z^2$ coefficient: $(4+b^2)+(9+4b^2)+24=117\Rightarrow b^2=16$, so $b=\pm4$.
Check: $z$ coefficient $-4(73)-6(20)=-412$ ✓ and constant $20\times73=1460$ ✓.
Zeroes: $2\pm4i,\ 3\pm8i$.
(ii) $P(z)=(z^2-4z+20)(z^2-6z+73)$.

items.q: The points $A,B,C$ and $D$ form a quadrilateral and represent the complex numbers $z_1,z_2,z_3$ and $z_4$ respectively. Given that $z_1-z_2+z_3-z_4=0$, determine what type of quadrilateral $ABCD$ is, giving reasons.
items.sol:
Rearrange: $z_1-z_2=z_4-z_3$, so $\overrightarrow{BA}=\overrightarrow{CD}$. One pair of opposite sides is equal in length and parallel, so $ABCD$ is a parallelogram.
(Equivalently $\frac{z_1+z_3}2=\frac{z_2+z_4}2$: the diagonals bisect each other.)

items.q:
(i) If $z=\cos\theta+i\sin\theta$, show that $z-\dfrac1z=2i\sin\theta$ and $z^n-\dfrac1{z^n}=2i\sin n\theta$. [2]
(ii) Hence show that $\sin^5\theta=\dfrac1{16}\sin5\theta-\dfrac5{16}\sin3\theta+\dfrac58\sin\theta$. [2]
items.sol:
(i) By De Moivre, $z^n=\cos n\theta+i\sin n\theta$ and $z^{-n}=\cos n\theta-i\sin n\theta$. Subtract to get $2i\sin n\theta$ ($n=1$ gives the first result).
(ii) $(2i\sin\theta)^5=\left(z-\frac1z\right)^5=\left(z^5-\frac1{z^5}\right)-5\left(z^3-\frac1{z^3}\right)+10\left(z-\frac1z\right)$.
So $32i\sin^5\theta=2i\sin5\theta-10i\sin3\theta+20i\sin\theta$. Divide by $32i$: $\sin^5\theta=\frac1{16}\sin5\theta-\frac5{16}\sin3\theta+\frac58\sin\theta$.

items.q:
Points $P$ and $Q$ represent the complex numbers $z$ and $w$ in the complex plane, and triangle $OPQ$ is equilateral (with $O\to P\to Q$ anticlockwise).
(i) Explain why $w=z\operatorname{cis}\dfrac\pi3$. [1]
(ii) Prove that $z^2+w^2=zw$. [2]
items.sol:
(i) $|OQ|=|OP|$ and $\angle POQ=\frac\pi3$, so $\overrightarrow{OQ}$ is $\overrightarrow{OP}$ rotated anticlockwise by $\frac\pi3$: $w=z\operatorname{cis}\frac\pi3$.
(ii) Let $\omega=\operatorname{cis}\frac\pi3$, so $\omega^3=-1$ and $\omega\ne-1$. Then $\omega^2-\omega+1=0$ (from $\omega^3+1=(\omega+1)(\omega^2-\omega+1)$).
$z^2+w^2-zw=z^2(1+\omega^2-\omega)=0$, so $z^2+w^2=zw$.

items.q:
The polynomial $P(z)=z^4-8z^3+pz^2+qz-80$ has a root $3+i$, where $p$ and $q$ are real.
(i) Find all the roots of $P(z)$. [3]
(ii) Write $P(z)$ as a product of two real quadratic factors. [1]
items.sol:
(i) $3-i$ is also a root, giving the factor $z^2-6z+10$. Let the other two roots be $\alpha,\beta$: sum of all roots $=8$, so $\alpha+\beta=2$. Product of all roots $=-80$, so $10\alpha\beta=-80$ and $\alpha\beta=-8$.
So $\alpha,\beta$ are roots of $z^2-2z-8=0$: $4$ and $-2$. Roots: $3\pm i,\ 4,\ -2$.
(ii) $P(z)=(z^2-6z+10)(z^2-2z-8)$.

items.q:
(i) Use De Moivre's theorem to show that $\cos3\theta=\cos^3\theta-3\cos\theta\sin^2\theta$ and $\sin3\theta=3\cos^2\theta\sin\theta-\sin^3\theta$. [2]
(ii) Deduce that $\tan3\theta=\dfrac{3\tan\theta-\tan^3\theta}{1-3\tan^2\theta}$. [1]
(iii) By letting $x=\tan\theta$, find the solutions of $x^3-3x^2-3x+1=0$ in exact trigonometric form. [3]
(iv) Hence show that $\tan\dfrac\pi{12}+\tan\dfrac{5\pi}{12}=4$. [1]
items.sol:
(i) $(\cos\theta+i\sin\theta)^3=\cos3\theta+i\sin3\theta$. Expand the left with $c=\cos\theta$, $s=\sin\theta$: $c^3+3ic^2s-3cs^2-is^3$. Equate real and imaginary parts.
(ii) Divide $\sin3\theta$ by $\cos3\theta$, then divide top and bottom by $\cos^3\theta$.
(iii) $x^3-3x^2-3x+1=0\iff3x-x^3=1-3x^2\iff\tan3\theta=1$ (for $1-3x^2\ne0$). So $3\theta=\frac\pi4+k\pi$, i.e. $\theta=\frac\pi{12},\frac{5\pi}{12},\frac{3\pi}4$. Solutions: $x=\tan\frac\pi{12},\ \tan\frac{5\pi}{12},\ \tan\frac{3\pi}4=-1$.
(iv) Sum of roots $=3$, so $\tan\frac\pi{12}+\tan\frac{5\pi}{12}-1=3$, giving $4$.

items.q: If $z=r(\cos\theta+i\sin\theta)$, use De Moivre's theorem to solve $z^3=\overline z$. Express your answer(s) in the form $a+ib$.
items.sol:
$r^3\operatorname{cis}3\theta=r\operatorname{cis}(-\theta)$. Either $r=0$ ($z=0$), or $r^2=1$ so $r=1$ and $3\theta=-\theta+2k\pi$, i.e. $\theta=\frac{k\pi}2$.
Solutions: $z=0,\ 1,\ i,\ -1,\ -i$.

items.q:
It is given that $z=2e^{\frac{i\pi}{12}}$ is a root of $z^4=a(1+\sqrt3\,i)$, where $a$ is real.
(i) Express $1+\sqrt3\,i$ in the form $re^{i\theta}$ where $r>0$ and $-\pi<\theta\le\pi$. [2]
(ii) Find the value of $a$. [1]
(iii) Find the other 3 roots in the form $re^{i\theta}$ where $r>0$ and $-\pi<\theta\le\pi$. [3]
items.sol:
(i) $1+\sqrt3\,i=2e^{\frac{i\pi}3}$.
(ii) $z^4=16e^{\frac{i\pi}3}=8\cdot2e^{\frac{i\pi}3}$, so $a=8$.
(iii) The roots are spaced $\frac\pi2$ apart on the circle $|z|=2$: $2e^{\frac{7i\pi}{12}},\ 2e^{-\frac{5i\pi}{12}},\ 2e^{-\frac{11i\pi}{12}}$.

items.q:
Given $z=\sqrt2+4i$ and $w=2+bi$, where $b\in\mathbb R$, such that $\arg w=\dfrac\pi4$.
(i) Show that $b=2$. [1]
(ii) Calculate $|zw|$. [1]
(iii) Find the value of $n$ for which $16|z|^n=81|w|^n$. [2]
items.sol:
(i) $\arg w=\frac\pi4$ means $\operatorname{Re}w=\operatorname{Im}w>0$, so $b=2$.
(ii) $|zw|=|z||w|=\sqrt{18}\cdot\sqrt8=12$.
(iii) $\left(\frac{|z|}{|w|}\right)^n=\frac{81}{16}$, and $\frac{|z|}{|w|}=\frac{3\sqrt2}{2\sqrt2}=\frac32$. So $n=4$.

items.q:
(i) Given $P_n(x)=(x-a_1)(x-a_2)\cdots(x-a_n)$, prove by mathematical induction that $\dfrac{P_n'(x)}{P_n(x)}=\dfrac1{x-a_1}+\dfrac1{x-a_2}+\cdots+\dfrac1{x-a_n}$ for $n\ge2$. [3]
(ii) Let $\omega$ be a (primitive) $n$th root of unity and $P(z)=(z-\omega)(z-\omega^2)\cdots(z-\omega^{n-1})$. By finding another expression for $P(z)$, or otherwise, show that $\dfrac1{1-\omega}+\dfrac1{1-\omega^2}+\cdots+\dfrac1{1-\omega^{n-1}}=\dfrac{n-1}2$. [3]
items.sol:
(i) $n=2$: $P_2'=(x-a_2)+(x-a_1)$, so $\frac{P_2'}{P_2}=\frac1{x-a_1}+\frac1{x-a_2}$ ✓. Assume true for $n=k$. Then $P_{k+1}=P_k\,(x-a_{k+1})$, so $P_{k+1}'=P_k'(x-a_{k+1})+P_k$ and $\frac{P_{k+1}'}{P_{k+1}}=\frac{P_k'}{P_k}+\frac1{x-a_{k+1}}$, which completes the induction.
(ii) The roots of $z^n-1$ are $1,\omega,\dots,\omega^{n-1}$, so $P(z)=\frac{z^n-1}{z-1}=1+z+\cdots+z^{n-1}$.
Then $P(1)=n$ and $P'(1)=1+2+\cdots+(n-1)=\frac{n(n-1)}2$.
By (i), $\frac{P'(1)}{P(1)}=\sum_{k=1}^{n-1}\frac1{1-\omega^k}$, which equals $\frac{n-1}2$.

items.q: Use the substitution $t=\tan\dfrac x2$ to evaluate $\displaystyle\int_0^{\frac\pi2}\frac{dx}{3\cos x-4\sin x+5}$.
items.sol:
$dx=\frac{2\,dt}{1+t^2}$, and the limits become $0\to1$.
Denominator $\times(1+t^2)$: $3(1-t^2)-8t+5(1+t^2)=2t^2-8t+8=2(t-2)^2$.
So the integral is $\displaystyle\int_0^1\frac{dt}{(t-2)^2}=\left[-\frac1{t-2}\right]_0^1=1-\frac12=\frac12$.

items.q: Use the substitution $t=\tan\dfrac x2$ to show that $\displaystyle\int_{\frac\pi3}^{\frac{2\pi}3}\frac{dx}{1+\sin x}=4-2\sqrt3$.
items.sol:
$1+\sin x=\frac{(1+t)^2}{1+t^2}$ and $dx=\frac{2\,dt}{1+t^2}$, so the integrand becomes $\frac{2}{(1+t)^2}$. The limits are $t=\frac1{\sqrt3}$ to $t=\sqrt3$.
$\left[-\frac2{1+t}\right]_{1/\sqrt3}^{\sqrt3}=-\frac2{1+\sqrt3}+\frac{2\sqrt3}{\sqrt3+1}=\frac{2(\sqrt3-1)}{\sqrt3+1}=(\sqrt3-1)^2=4-2\sqrt3$.

items.q: By using the substitution $t=\tan\theta$, or otherwise, evaluate $\displaystyle\int_0^{\frac\pi4}\frac{4}{5-3\cos2\theta}\,d\theta$.
items.sol:
$\cos2\theta=\frac{1-t^2}{1+t^2}$ and $d\theta=\frac{dt}{1+t^2}$; the limits become $0\to1$.
$5(1+t^2)-3(1-t^2)=2+8t^2$, so the integral is $\displaystyle\int_0^1\frac{4\,dt}{2+8t^2}=\int_0^1\frac{2\,dt}{1+4t^2}=\left[\tan^{-1}2t\right]_0^1=\tan^{-1}2$.

items.q:
(i) Given that $t=\tan\left(\dfrac\theta2\right)$, show that $\cos\left(\dfrac\theta2\right)=\dfrac1{\sqrt{1+t^2}}$ (for $\cos\frac\theta2>0$). [1]
(ii) Hence, or otherwise, solve $\sin\theta-\cos\left(\dfrac\theta2\right)=0$ for $0\le\theta\le2\pi$. [3]
items.sol:
(i) $1+t^2=\sec^2\frac\theta2$, so $\cos\frac\theta2=\frac1{\sqrt{1+t^2}}$ when it is positive.
(ii) $2\sin\frac\theta2\cos\frac\theta2-\cos\frac\theta2=0\Rightarrow\cos\frac\theta2\left(2\sin\frac\theta2-1\right)=0$.
$\cos\frac\theta2=0\Rightarrow\theta=\pi$. $\sin\frac\theta2=\frac12\Rightarrow\frac\theta2=\frac\pi6,\frac{5\pi}6\Rightarrow\theta=\frac\pi3,\frac{5\pi}3$.
So $\theta=\frac\pi3,\ \pi,\ \frac{5\pi}3$. (Watch out: a pure $t$-substitution loses $\theta=\pi$.)

items.q: By letting $t=\tan\dfrac x2$, solve $\sin x+\cos x=-1$ for $0\le x\le2\pi$.
items.sol:
$\frac{2t}{1+t^2}+\frac{1-t^2}{1+t^2}=-1\Rightarrow2t+1-t^2=-1-t^2\Rightarrow t=-1$, so $\frac x2=\frac{3\pi}4$ and $x=\frac{3\pi}2$.
Test the excluded value $x=\pi$ (where $t$ is undefined): $\sin\pi+\cos\pi=-1$ ✓.
So $x=\pi$ or $x=\frac{3\pi}2$.

items.q:
(i) Show that $\dfrac{\sin\theta+\sin3\theta+\sin5\theta}{\cos\theta+\cos3\theta+\cos5\theta}=\tan3\theta$. [2]
(ii) Hence solve $\dfrac{\sin\theta+\sin3\theta+\sin5\theta}{\cos\theta+\cos3\theta+\cos5\theta}=1$ for $0\le\theta\le2\pi$. [1]
items.sol:
(i) Sums to products: $\sin5\theta+\sin\theta=2\sin3\theta\cos2\theta$ and $\cos5\theta+\cos\theta=2\cos3\theta\cos2\theta$. So the fraction is $\frac{\sin3\theta(2\cos2\theta+1)}{\cos3\theta(2\cos2\theta+1)}=\tan3\theta$.
(ii) $\tan3\theta=1\Rightarrow3\theta=\frac\pi4+k\pi\Rightarrow\theta=\frac\pi{12},\frac{5\pi}{12},\frac{3\pi}4,\frac{13\pi}{12},\frac{17\pi}{12},\frac{7\pi}4$. None of these makes $2\cos2\theta+1=0$ (which needs $\theta=\frac\pi3,\frac{2\pi}3,\dots$), so all six are valid.

items.q:
(i) Prove that $\tan4\theta-\tan\theta=\dfrac{\sin3\theta}{\cos4\theta\cos\theta}$. [2]
(ii) Hence solve $\tan4\theta=\tan\theta$ for $0\le\theta\le\pi$. [2]
items.sol:
(i) $\frac{\sin4\theta}{\cos4\theta}-\frac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}=\frac{\sin4\theta\cos\theta-\cos4\theta\sin\theta}{\cos4\theta\cos\theta}=\frac{\sin3\theta}{\cos4\theta\cos\theta}$.
(ii) We need $\sin3\theta=0$ with $\cos4\theta\cos\theta\ne0$: $\theta=0,\frac\pi3,\frac{2\pi}3,\pi$. All of these keep both tangents defined.

items.q:
(i) Show that $\cos x+\cos5x=2\cos3x\cos2x$. [1]
(ii) Hence, or otherwise, solve $\cos x+\cos5x=\cos2x$ for $x\in[0,\pi]$. [2]
items.sol:
(i) $\cos A+\cos B=2\cos\frac{A+B}2\cos\frac{A-B}2$ with $A=5x$, $B=x$.
(ii) $\cos2x(2\cos3x-1)=0$.
$\cos2x=0\Rightarrow x=\frac\pi4,\frac{3\pi}4$. $\cos3x=\frac12$ with $3x\in[0,3\pi]$ gives $3x=\frac\pi3,\frac{5\pi}3,\frac{7\pi}3\Rightarrow x=\frac\pi9,\frac{5\pi}9,\frac{7\pi}9$.
So $x=\frac\pi9,\frac\pi4,\frac{5\pi}9,\frac{3\pi}4,\frac{7\pi}9$.

items.q: Use sums to products to simplify, and hence solve, $\sin5x+\sin x=\sin3x$ for $0\le x\le\pi$.
items.sol:
$\sin5x+\sin x=2\sin3x\cos2x$, so $\sin3x(2\cos2x-1)=0$.
$\sin3x=0\Rightarrow x=0,\frac\pi3,\frac{2\pi}3,\pi$. $\cos2x=\frac12\Rightarrow x=\frac\pi6,\frac{5\pi}6$.
So $x=0,\frac\pi6,\frac\pi3,\frac{2\pi}3,\frac{5\pi}6,\pi$.

items.q: Use the $t=\tan\dfrac x2$ results to show that $\cot\dfrac x2+\tan\dfrac x2=2\operatorname{cosec}x$.
items.sol: LHS $=\frac1t+t=\frac{1+t^2}t$. RHS $=\frac2{\sin x}=\frac{2}{\frac{2t}{1+t^2}}=\frac{1+t^2}t$. So LHS $=$ RHS.

items.q: Show that $\dfrac{\sin2x}{1+\cos2x}=\tan x$.
items.sol:
$\frac{2\sin x\cos x}{1+(2\cos^2x-1)}=\frac{2\sin x\cos x}{2\cos^2x}=\tan x$.
(This is the half-angle result $\tan\frac\theta2=\frac{\sin\theta}{1+\cos\theta}$ with $\theta=2x$.)

items.q: Using $t=\tan\dfrac\theta2$, solve $2\cos\theta+3\sin\theta=-2$ for $0\le\theta\le2\pi$.
items.sol:
$2(1-t^2)+6t=-2(1+t^2)\Rightarrow6t=-4\Rightarrow t=-\frac23$. With $\frac\theta2\in(0,\pi)$, $\frac\theta2=\pi-\tan^{-1}\frac23$, so $\theta=2\pi-2\tan^{-1}\frac23\approx5.11$.
Test $\theta=\pi$ (where $t$ is undefined): $2(-1)+0=-2$ ✓.
So $\theta=\pi$ or $\theta=2\pi-2\tan^{-1}\frac23$.

items.q:
Given that $t=\tan\dfrac\pi8$:
(i) Show that $\dfrac{2t}{1-t^2}=1$. [1]
(ii) Hence find the exact value of $\tan\dfrac\pi8$. [2]
items.sol:
(i) $\frac{2t}{1-t^2}=\tan\left(2\cdot\frac\pi8\right)=\tan\frac\pi4=1$.
(ii) $t^2+2t-1=0\Rightarrow t=-1\pm\sqrt2$. Since $\tan\frac\pi8>0$, $\tan\frac\pi8=\sqrt2-1$.

items.q: By letting $t=\tan\dfrac x2$, solve $4\sin x-3\cos x=3$ for $0\le x\le2\pi$.
items.sol:
$8t-3(1-t^2)=3(1+t^2)\Rightarrow8t=6\Rightarrow t=\frac34$, so $x=2\tan^{-1}\frac34\approx1.29$.
Test $x=\pi$: $4(0)-3(-1)=3$ ✓.
So $x=2\tan^{-1}\frac34$ or $x=\pi$.

items.q: Use the product-to-sum identity to write $\cos\theta\sin2\theta$ as a sum in simplest form.
items.sol: $\sin A\cos B=\frac12[\sin(A+B)+\sin(A-B)]$ with $A=2\theta$, $B=\theta$: $\cos\theta\sin2\theta=\frac12(\sin3\theta+\sin\theta)$.

items.source: North Sydney Boys 2021 Ext 1 Trial, Q13(c)
items.q: Using sums to products, solve $\cos x+\cos2x+\cos3x=0$ for $0\le x\le2\pi$.
items.sol:
$\cos3x+\cos x=2\cos2x\cos x$, so $\cos2x(2\cos x+1)=0$.
$\cos2x=0\Rightarrow x=\frac\pi4,\frac{3\pi}4,\frac{5\pi}4,\frac{7\pi}4$. $\cos x=-\frac12\Rightarrow x=\frac{2\pi}3,\frac{4\pi}3$.

items.q: Prove that $\sin x+\sin2x+\sin3x=\sin2x\,(2\cos x+1)$.
items.sol: $\sin3x+\sin x=2\sin2x\cos x$, so LHS $=2\sin2x\cos x+\sin2x=\sin2x(2\cos x+1)$.

items.q: Find the $y$-intercept of the tangent to $y=x^2\sin^{-1}x$ at the point $\left(\dfrac12,\dfrac\pi{24}\right)$.
items.sol:
$y'=2x\sin^{-1}x+\frac{x^2}{\sqrt{1-x^2}}$. At $x=\frac12$: $m=\frac\pi6+\frac{1/4}{\sqrt3/2}=\frac\pi6+\frac{\sqrt3}6$.
$y$-intercept $=\frac\pi{24}-\frac12m=\frac\pi{24}-\frac\pi{12}-\frac{\sqrt3}{12}=-\frac\pi{24}-\frac{\sqrt3}{12}$.

items.q:
Let $z_1$ and $z_2$ be two non-zero complex numbers such that $z_1+z_2+1=0$.
(i) Show that $|z_1|=|z_2|=1\ \Rightarrow\ \dfrac1{z_1}+\dfrac1{z_2}+1=0$. [2]
(ii) Also show that $\dfrac1{z_1}+\dfrac1{z_2}+1=0\ \Rightarrow\ |z_1|=|z_2|=1$. [2]
(iii) Hence or otherwise show that $|z_1|=|z_2|=1\ \Rightarrow\ z_1^2+z_2^2+1=0$. [1]
items.sol:
(i) $|z|=1$ means $\frac1z=\overline z$. So $\frac1{z_1}+\frac1{z_2}+1=\overline{z_1+z_2+1}=\overline0=0$.
(ii) $\frac{z_1+z_2}{z_1z_2}=-1$ and $z_1+z_2=-1$, so $z_1z_2=1$. Then $z_1,z_2$ are the roots of $z^2+z+1=0$, i.e. $\operatorname{cis}(\pm\frac{2\pi}3)$, both of modulus 1.
(iii) From (i) and (ii), $z_1+z_2=-1$ and $z_1z_2=1$. So $z_1^2+z_2^2=(z_1+z_2)^2-2z_1z_2=1-2=-1$, giving $z_1^2+z_2^2+1=0$.

items.q: Let $\omega$ be the complex number satisfying $\omega^3=1$ and $\operatorname{Im}(\omega)>0$. The cubic $P(z)=z^3+az^2+bz+c$ has zeros $1$, $-\omega$ and $-\overline\omega$. Find $a$, $b$ and $c$.
items.sol:
$\omega=-\frac12+\frac{\sqrt3}2i$, so $-\omega-\overline\omega=-2\operatorname{Re}\omega=1$ and $(-\omega)(-\overline\omega)=|\omega|^2=1$.
Sum of zeros: $1+1=2=-a$, so $a=-2$.
Sum of pairs: $1\cdot1+1=2=b$.
Product: $1\cdot1=1=-c$, so $c=-1$.
$P(z)=z^3-2z^2+2z-1$ (check: $P(1)=0$ ✓).

items.q:
Consider the equation $z^2-2(1+2i)z+(1+i)=0$.
(i) Show that $\left(z-(1+2i)\right)^2=-4+3i$. [1]
(ii) Hence solve $z^2-2(1+2i)z+(1+i)=0$. [3]

Let $\omega$ be a cube root of unity, $\omega\ne1$.
(i) Show that $1+\omega+\omega^2=0$. [1]
(ii) Consider $\varphi_n(x)=x^{4n+1}+(x+1)^{2n-1}$, where $n$ is a positive integer. Show that $\varphi_n(\omega)=0$ and $\varphi_n(\omega^2)=0$. [4]
(iii) Hence show that $x^2+x+1$ is a factor of $\varphi_n(x)$. [2]
items.sol:
(i) $\omega^3-1=(\omega-1)(\omega^2+\omega+1)=0$ with $\omega\ne1$.
(ii) $\omega+1=-\omega^2$, so $(\omega+1)^{2n-1}=(-1)^{2n-1}\omega^{4n-2}=-\omega^{4n-2}$. Then $\varphi_n(\omega)=\omega^{4n+1}-\omega^{4n-2}=\omega^{4n-2}(\omega^3-1)=0$.
Similarly $\omega^2+1=-\omega$, so $\varphi_n(\omega^2)=\omega^{8n+2}-\omega^{2n-1}=\omega^{2n-1}(\omega^{6n+3}-1)=0$, since $\omega^{6n+3}=(\omega^3)^{2n+1}=1$.
(iii) $x^2+x+1=(x-\omega)(x-\omega^2)$ with $\omega\ne\omega^2$, and both are zeros of $\varphi_n$. By the factor theorem, $x^2+x+1$ divides $\varphi_n(x)$.

items.q:
(i) Write $w=\dfrac{8-2i}{5+3i}$ in the form $x+iy$. [1]
(ii) Find the argument of $w$. [1]
(iii) Hence, or otherwise, find the possible values of the positive integer $n$ for which $w^n$ is purely real. [2]
items.sol:
(i) $w=\frac{(8-2i)(5-3i)}{34}=\frac{34-34i}{34}=1-i$.
(ii) $\arg w=-\frac\pi4$.
(iii) $w^n=(\sqrt2)^n\operatorname{cis}\left(-\frac{n\pi}4\right)$ is real when $\frac{n\pi}4$ is a multiple of $\pi$: $n=4,8,12,\dots$ (multiples of 4).

items.q:
(Varignon's theorem) $ABCD$ is any quadrilateral, and $E,F,G,H$ are the midpoints of $AD$, $DC$, $CB$ and $BA$. Let $\overrightarrow{BA}=\mathbf u$, $\overrightarrow{AD}=\mathbf v$, $\overrightarrow{DC}=\mathbf w$ and $\overrightarrow{CB}=\mathbf z$.
(i) Explain why $\mathbf u+\mathbf v+\mathbf w+\mathbf z=\mathbf 0$. [1]
(ii) Show that $\overrightarrow{HE}=\frac12(\mathbf u+\mathbf v)$. [1]
(iii) Show that $\overrightarrow{GF}=\frac12(\mathbf u+\mathbf v)$ too, and hence that $EFGH$ is a parallelogram. [2]
items.sol:
(i) $B\to A\to D\to C\to B$ is a closed path, so the vectors sum to zero.
(ii) $\overrightarrow{HE}=\overrightarrow{HA}+\overrightarrow{AE}=\frac12\mathbf u+\frac12\mathbf v$.
(iii) $\overrightarrow{GF}=\overrightarrow{GC}+\overrightarrow{CF}=-\frac12\mathbf z-\frac12\mathbf w=\frac12(\mathbf u+\mathbf v)$ by (i). So $\overrightarrow{HE}=\overrightarrow{GF}$: one pair of opposite sides is equal and parallel, so $EFGH$ is a parallelogram.

items.q:
$X$ lies on interval $AB$ with $AX:XB=m:n$ ($m,n>0$, $m\ne n$). Let $\overrightarrow{OA}=\mathbf a$ and $\overrightarrow{OB}=\mathbf b$.
(i) Show that $\overrightarrow{OX}=\dfrac{n\mathbf a+m\mathbf b}{m+n}$. [2]
(ii) $Y$ is on line $AB$ with $\overrightarrow{OY}=\dfrac{n\mathbf a-m\mathbf b}{n-m}$ (do not prove this). If $OX\perp OY$, show that $n|\mathbf a|=m|\mathbf b|$. [2]
items.sol:
(i) $\overrightarrow{OX}=\mathbf a+\frac m{m+n}(\mathbf b-\mathbf a)=\frac{n\mathbf a+m\mathbf b}{m+n}$.
(ii) Perpendicular means $(n\mathbf a+m\mathbf b)\cdot(n\mathbf a-m\mathbf b)=0$, so $n^2|\mathbf a|^2-m^2|\mathbf b|^2=0$. Since lengths are positive, $n|\mathbf a|=m|\mathbf b|$.

items.q:
The complex number $w$ lies on the unit circle with $\operatorname{Arg}(w)=\theta$.
(i) Show that $\dfrac{1+w}{1-w}=i\cot\dfrac\theta2$. [3]
(ii) Hence solve $\left(\dfrac{z-1}{z+1}\right)^8=-1$. [3]
items.sol:
(i) Factor out $e^{i\theta/2}$: $\frac{1+w}{1-w}=\frac{e^{-i\theta/2}+e^{i\theta/2}}{e^{-i\theta/2}-e^{i\theta/2}}=\frac{2\cos\frac\theta2}{-2i\sin\frac\theta2}=i\cot\frac\theta2$.
(ii) Let $w=\frac{z-1}{z+1}$, so $w^8=-1$ and $w=\operatorname{cis}\frac{(2k+1)\pi}8$ for $k=0,\dots,7$ (on the unit circle, $w\ne1$).
Solving for $z$: $z=\frac{1+w}{1-w}=i\cot\frac{(2k+1)\pi}{16}$, $k=0,1,\dots,7$.

items.q:
Line $r_1$: $\mathbf r=\mathbf i+2\mathbf k+\lambda(2\mathbf i+3\mathbf j-\mathbf k)$, $\lambda\in\mathbb R$. Line $r_2$: $\dfrac{x+1}1=\dfrac{y-4}1=\dfrac{z-1}3$.
(i) Show that $r_2$ is $\mathbf r=-\mathbf i+4\mathbf j+\mathbf k+\mu(\mathbf i+\mathbf j+3\mathbf k)$, $\mu\in\mathbb R$. [1]
(ii) Show that $r_1$ and $r_2$ do not intersect. [3]
(iii) $A$ lies on $r_1$ with $\lambda=p$ and $B$ on $r_2$ with $\mu=q$. Write $\overrightarrow{AB}$ as a column vector. [1]
items.sol:
(i) Set each fraction equal to $\mu$: $x=-1+\mu$, $y=4+\mu$, $z=1+3\mu$.
(ii) Equate components: $1+2\lambda=-1+\mu$, $3\lambda=4+\mu$, $2-\lambda=1+3\mu$. The first two give $\lambda=6$, $\mu=14$, but then the third gives $-4\ne43$. So there is no common point (and the directions aren't parallel, so the lines are skew).
(iii) $\overrightarrow{AB}=\begin{pmatrix}-1+q\\4+q\\1+3q\end{pmatrix}-\begin{pmatrix}1+2p\\3p\\2-p\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}q-2p-2\\q-3p+4\\3q+p-1\end{pmatrix}$.

items.q:
$L_1:\ \mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}3\\2\\-1\end{pmatrix}+\lambda\begin{pmatrix}2\\-1\\1\end{pmatrix}$ and $L_2:\ \mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}-1\\1\\0\end{pmatrix}+\mu\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\\-1\end{pmatrix}$.
(i) Show that $L_1$ and $L_2$ intersect and are perpendicular, and state the point of intersection. [3]
(ii) Deduce that the plane containing $L_1$ and $L_2$ is $\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}1\\3\\-2\end{pmatrix}+a\begin{pmatrix}2\\-1\\1\end{pmatrix}+b\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\\-1\end{pmatrix}$, and hence that it has equation $y+z=1$. [2]
items.sol:
(i) $3+2\lambda=-1+\mu$, $2-\lambda=1+\mu$, $-1+\lambda=-\mu$. The third gives $\mu=1-\lambda$, which makes the second an identity. The first then gives $3+2\lambda=-\lambda$, so $\lambda=-1$, $\mu=2$. Intersection: $(1,3,-2)$.
$(2,-1,1)\cdot(1,1,-1)=2-1-1=0$, so they are perpendicular.
(ii) The plane passes through $(1,3,-2)$ and contains both direction vectors. Then $y=3-a+b$ and $z=-2+a-b$, so $y+z=1$.

items.q: Consider $f(x)=x^4+2x^3+2x^2+26x+169$. Given $f(2+3i)=0$, fully factorise $f(x)$ over the complex numbers.
items.sol:
$2\pm3i$ are zeros, giving the factor $x^2-4x+13$. Divide (or match coefficients): $f(x)=(x^2-4x+13)(x^2+6x+13)$. The second factor has zeros $-3\pm2i$.
$f(x)=(x-2-3i)(x-2+3i)(x+3-2i)(x+3+2i)$.

items.q: Find the range of values of $p\in\mathbb R$ such that $x^4-px^3+px-1=0$ has exactly one pair of complex conjugate (non-real) roots.
items.sol: Factorise: $x^4-1-px(x^2-1)=(x^2-1)(x^2-px+1)$. The roots $\pm1$ are real, so we need $x^2-px+1$ to have non-real roots: $\Delta=p^2-4<0$, i.e. $-2<p<2$.

items.q: Points $A$ and $B$ represent $z_A=1+i$ and $z_B=-4$. The isosceles triangle $ABC$ is right-angled at $C$. Find the possible values of $z_C$.
items.sol:
$C$ lies on the perpendicular bisector of $AB$, at distance $\frac12|AB|$ from the midpoint $M=\frac{-3+i}2$. So $z_C=M\pm\frac i2(z_A-z_B)=\frac{-3+i}2\pm\frac{i(5+i)}2$.
$z_C=-2+3i$ or $z_C=-1-2i$.

items.q:
Consider the equation $z^5=1$.
(i) Write down, in polar form, the five roots of $z^5=1$. [2]
(ii) Show that for $z\ne1$: $\dfrac{z^5-1}{z-1}=\left(z^2-2z\cos\dfrac{2\pi}5+1\right)\left(z^2-2z\cos\dfrac{4\pi}5+1\right)$. [2]
(iii) Deduce that $\cos\dfrac{2\pi}5$ and $\cos\dfrac{4\pi}5$ are roots of $4x^2+2x-1=0$. [3]
items.sol:
(i) $z=\operatorname{cis}\frac{2k\pi}5$, $k=0,\pm1,\pm2$.
(ii) The non-real roots pair into conjugates: $(z-\operatorname{cis}\alpha)(z-\operatorname{cis}(-\alpha))=z^2-2z\cos\alpha+1$ for $\alpha=\frac{2\pi}5,\frac{4\pi}5$. Their product is $\frac{z^5-1}{z-1}$.
(iii) Let $a=\cos\frac{2\pi}5$ and $b=\cos\frac{4\pi}5$. Expanding gives $z^4-2(a+b)z^3+(2+4ab)z^2-2(a+b)z+1=z^4+z^3+z^2+z+1$. So $a+b=-\frac12$ and $ab=-\frac14$, which means $a$ and $b$ are roots of $x^2+\frac12x-\frac14=0$, i.e. $4x^2+2x-1=0$.

items.q:
(i) Show that $\sec\left(2\sin^{-1}x\right)$ can be expressed as $\dfrac1{1-2x^2}$. [2]
(ii) Hence, or otherwise, solve $\sec\left(2\sin^{-1}x\right)=-2$. [2]
items.sol:
(i) Let $\alpha=\sin^{-1}x$. Then $\cos2\alpha=1-2\sin^2\alpha=1-2x^2$, so $\sec2\alpha=\frac1{1-2x^2}$.
(ii) $1-2x^2=-\frac12\Rightarrow x^2=\frac34\Rightarrow x=\pm\frac{\sqrt3}2$. Check $x=\frac{\sqrt3}2$: $2\cdot\frac\pi3=\frac{2\pi}3$ and $\sec\frac{2\pi}3=-2$ ✓. Since sec is even, $x=-\frac{\sqrt3}2$ also works.

items.source: St George Girls 2023 Ext 1 Trial (inverse trig)
items.q: Find the exact value of $\cos^{-1}\left(\sin\dfrac{4\pi}3\right)$.
items.sol: $\sin\frac{4\pi}3=-\frac{\sqrt3}2$, and $\cos^{-1}\left(-\frac{\sqrt3}2\right)=\pi-\frac\pi6=\frac{5\pi}6$.

items.source: St George Girls 2026 Ext 1 Trial, Q14(a)
items.q: Solve for $x$: $\sin^{-1}x-\cos^{-1}x=\dfrac\pi6$.
items.sol: Use $\cos^{-1}x=\frac\pi2-\sin^{-1}x$: $2\sin^{-1}x-\frac\pi2=\frac\pi6\Rightarrow\sin^{-1}x=\frac\pi3\Rightarrow x=\frac{\sqrt3}2$.

items.source: North Sydney Boys 2023 Ext 1 Trial, Q11(c)
items.q: By using the substitution $u=\tan^{-1}x$, find $\displaystyle\int\frac{e^{\tan^{-1}x}}{1+x^2}\,dx$.
items.sol: $du=\frac{dx}{1+x^2}$, so the integral is $\int e^u\,du=e^{\tan^{-1}x}+C$.

items.source: North Sydney Boys 2024 Ext 1 Trial, Q11(b)
items.q: Find the exact value of $\sin\left(2\cos^{-1}\dfrac23\right)$.
items.sol: Let $\theta=\cos^{-1}\frac23\in[0,\pi]$, so $\sin\theta=\frac{\sqrt5}3$. Then $\sin2\theta=2\cdot\frac{\sqrt5}3\cdot\frac23=\frac{4\sqrt5}9$.

items.q:
Points $A$ and $B$ have position vectors $\overrightarrow{OA}=3\mathbf i+\mathbf j$ and $\overrightarrow{OB}=2\mathbf j$.
(i) Find $\overrightarrow{AB}$, and hence the projection of $\overrightarrow{AO}$ onto $\overrightarrow{AB}$. [2]
(ii) $P$ is the point on $AB$ such that $OP\perp AB$. Find $\overrightarrow{OP}$. [2]
items.sol:
(i) $\overrightarrow{AB}=-3\mathbf i+\mathbf j$ and $\overrightarrow{AO}=-3\mathbf i-\mathbf j$. The projection is $\frac{\overrightarrow{AO}\cdot\overrightarrow{AB}}{|\overrightarrow{AB}|^2}\overrightarrow{AB}=\frac{9-1}{10}(-3\mathbf i+\mathbf j)=-\frac{12}5\mathbf i+\frac45\mathbf j$.
(ii) $P$ is the foot of the perpendicular, so $\overrightarrow{AP}$ is that projection: $\overrightarrow{OP}=\overrightarrow{OA}+\overrightarrow{AP}=\frac35\mathbf i+\frac95\mathbf j$.
Check: $\overrightarrow{OP}\cdot\overrightarrow{AB}=-\frac95+\frac95=0$ ✓

items.q: For two distinct values of $k$, the position vectors $\overrightarrow{OA}=3\mathbf i-\mathbf j$ and $\overrightarrow{OB}=2\mathbf i+k\mathbf j$ form adjacent sides of a rhombus. Find the two possible areas of the rhombus.
items.sol:
A rhombus needs equal adjacent sides: $|\overrightarrow{OA}|^2=|\overrightarrow{OB}|^2\Rightarrow10=4+k^2\Rightarrow k=\pm\sqrt6$.
Area $=|OA||OB|\sin\theta=|3k-(-1)(2)|=|3k+2|$. You can get this from $\cos\theta=\frac{6-k}{10}$ too.
$k=\sqrt6$: area $3\sqrt6+2$. $k=-\sqrt6$: area $3\sqrt6-2$.

items.q:
$P$ has position vector $3\mathbf i+4\mathbf j$, and the line $l$ has equation $x-2y=0$.
(i) Find the projection of $\overrightarrow{OP}$ onto the line $l$. [2]
(ii) Hence find the exact perpendicular distance from $P$ to $l$. [1]
items.sol:
(i) $l$ passes through $O$ with direction $2\mathbf i+\mathbf j$. Projection $=\frac{6+4}{5}(2\mathbf i+\mathbf j)=4\mathbf i+2\mathbf j$.
(ii) Distance $=|(3\mathbf i+4\mathbf j)-(4\mathbf i+2\mathbf j)|=|-\mathbf i+2\mathbf j|=\sqrt5$.
